Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.", "commands": [ { "keystrokes": "ls -la\n", "duration": 0.1 }, { "keystrokes": "cd project\n", "duration": 0.1 } ], "task_complete": true } Required fields: - "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation - "plan": Your plan for the next steps - "commands": Array of command objects to execute Optional fields: - "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present) Command object structure: - "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required) - "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present) IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal: - You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute. - For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences: - C-c for Ctrl+C - C-d for Ctrl+D The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary. It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status. Important notes: - Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal - Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command - Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated - The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings - Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action Task Description: Implement a sparse matrix iterative solver toolkit in C called `nlsolve`. The tool reads a linear system Ax = b from files and solves it using iterative methods, outputting the solution vector and convergence statistics. It also supports matrix analysis and bandwidth-reducing reordering. ## Matrix Format Use the Matrix Market coordinate format (.mtx). The format is: ``` %%MatrixMarket matrix coordinate real symmetric % optional comment lines ROWS COLS NNZ row col value row col value ... ``` For symmetric matrices, only the lower triangle (including diagonal) is stored. The tool must expand symmetric storage internally. Row and column indices are 1-based in the file. Also support `general` symmetry (all entries explicitly listed). ## Vector Format Plain text, one value per line: ``` N value1 value2 ... ``` The first line is the dimension, followed by N floating-point values. ## Solvers Support two iterative solvers: 1. **Conjugate Gradient (CG)** - for symmetric positive definite (SPD) systems, with residual-based convergence: stop when `||r_k||_2 / ||b||_2 < tol`. 2. **BiCGSTAB** - for general non-symmetric systems, with the same relative residual convergence criterion. ## Preconditioners Implement three preconditioners: 1. **Jacobi** - diagonal scaling: M = diag(A) 2. **SSOR** - Symmetric Successive Over-Relaxation with omega=1.2. 3. **IC(0)** - Incomplete Cholesky preconditioning with zero fill-in, using the lower-triangular sparsity pattern of A. Only valid for SPD matrices used with CG. ## Matrix Reordering When `--reorder rcm` is specified, apply Reverse Cuthill-McKee (RCM) reordering before solving. The matrix graph should be ordered deterministically by node degree and original node index, then rows and columns of A and entries of b should be permuted consistently. The reported solution must always be converted back to the original variable ordering before output. ## Matrix Analysis When `--analyze` is specified instead of `--solver`, print analysis to stdout: ``` dimension: nonzeros: symmetric: bandwidth: profile:

diag_dominant: ``` Where: - **bandwidth** B = max over all non-zero a_{ij} of |i - j| - **profile** P = sum over all rows i of (i - min column index in row i). Only count rows that have at least one off-diagonal entry; rows with only a diagonal entry contribute 0. - **diag_dominant**: "strict" if |a_{ii}| > sum of |a_{ij}| for all j != i, for every row; "weak" if |a_{ii}| >= sum for every row (but not all strict); "no" otherwise. ## Matrix Generator Include a built-in 2D Laplacian matrix generator. For an n*n grid, produce the standard 5-point stencil matrix of dimension n^2 * n^2. The diagonal is 4.0, and off-diagonals are -1.0 for adjacent grid points (both within-row and between-row connections). Write the generated matrix as Matrix Market `real symmetric` coordinate data using lower-triangle storage. Also include a 3D Laplacian generator for an n*n*n grid, producing the standard 7-point stencil matrix of dimension n^3 * n^3. The diagonal is 6.0, and off-diagonals are -1.0 for the 6 neighbors (x+1, x-1, y+1, y-1, z+1, z-1). Write the generated matrix as Matrix Market `real symmetric` coordinate data using lower-triangle storage. ## Command-Line Interface ``` nlsolve --input --rhs --solver \ --precond --tol --maxiter \ [--reorder rcm] [--history] nlsolve --input --analyze nlsolve --generate-laplacian --output nlsolve --generate-laplacian3d --output nlsolve --generate-rhs --output ``` The `--generate-rhs` command produces a vector of dimension N where the i-th value (for i = 1, 2, ..., N) is sin(i * pi / (N+1)). The `--history` flag causes the solver to print one line per iteration before the solution output: `iter : residual = ` using `%.6e` format for the residual. Iteration numbering starts at 1. ## Output Format For solve mode, print to stdout: ``` solver: preconditioner: dimension: reordering: iterations: residual_norm: converged: solution: x[0] = x[1] = ... x[N-1] = ``` All floating-point values in the output use `%.6e` format (6 decimal places, scientific notation). For generate modes, write the file and print nothing to stdout. ## Build The project must compile with `make` producing the `nlsolve` binary. A simple Makefile with `gcc -O2 -lm` is sufficient. ## Defaults - `--tol` defaults to `1e-6` - `--maxiter` defaults to `10000` - `--precond` defaults to `none` - `--reorder` defaults to `none` (no reordering) ======================================================================== [RepoTrace] Repository guidance for the current request (round 1) The notes below summarize structural centrality and cross-round state.
